summary: This informational document describes an architecture for managing networks using NETCONF and YANG. NETCONF accesses device configuration and operations, while YANG defines the data and operations it carries. Together they allow standard modules for device management.

eli5.summary: One tool carries messages to devices and another describes the form those messages take. This explains how they fit together like a postal service and its forms.

questions: how do netconf and yang work together
subtitle: How NETCONF carries management operations and YANG describes the data, so network management applications can work together.

tldr.problem: Network operators needed better configuration management, with transactions, rollback and a clear split between configuration and other data. NETCONF carried data but had no standard way to define what that data looks like.
tldr.mechanism: NETCONF provides XML-based RPC operations over a secure, connection-oriented transport, and YANG defines the data models and operations carried in them, acting as a contract between client and server.
tldr.outcome: Standard YANG modules can give interoperability across devices while vendors extend them with their own. The RFC also gives modelers guidance on defaults, compliance and separating configuration from operational state.

today: RFC 6244 is an Informational document with no obsoleting or updating RFCs listed. It describes the NETCONF and YANG architecture as of 2011, built on RFC 4741 and RFC 6020, and states that it has no security impact on the Internet.

sections.title: Where NETCONF and YANG Came From
sections.content:
In June 2002 the Internet Architecture Board held a workshop on network management (RFC 3535). Operators asked for transactions, rollback, low implementation cost, saving and restoring configuration, and a clear distinction between configuration data and other data. The NETCONF working group was formed and created the NETCONF protocol (RFC 4741).

NETCONF defines a small set of operations and is deliberately data model agnostic, so it can carry any data. That left a gap: with no way to define data models, it could not be used for standards-based work. XML Schema and DSDL were considered and rejected, because defining a protocol's data differs from defining a static XML document. The NETMOD working group produced YANG (RFC 6020) in 2008 and 2009 to fill the gap.
sections.eli5: Operators said their tools were hard to use. First came a way to send messages to devices, then a way to describe what those messages should say.

sections.title: NETCONF: Operations and Datastores
sections.content:
NETCONF defines an XML-based remote procedure call (RPC) mechanism. Configuration data and operations travel as requests and replies over a connection-oriented transport. Configuration lives in datastores: a device may have a separate "startup" datastore, a writable "running" datastore, and a "candidate" datastore where changes do not affect the device until a commit.

Devices announce their capabilities, including operations, datastores and data models, in the <hello> message at session setup. NETCONF can also send asynchronous notifications from server to client (RFC 5277).

Any transport that is connection-oriented and provides authentication, integrity and confidentiality can be used. SSH is the mandatory transport (RFC 4742); SOAP, BEEP and TLS mappings also exist.
sections.eli5: A device keeps several notebooks of settings. You can scribble in a draft notebook and only copy it into the live one when you say commit.

sections.title: YANG: Modeling the Data
sections.content:
YANG is a data modeling language for NETCONF. A module defines a data model identified by a namespace URI, built from containers, lists and leafs. It also defines constraints that rule out impossible data: the type statement is the main one, with others such as range, length, mandatory, must and when. The must and when statements use XPath, but neither side is required to implement XPath itself.

Flexibility comes from union types, choice and feature. A deviation lets a device declare where it does not faithfully implement a module, rather than leaving that to be found through run-time errors.

A published YANG module acts as a contract between client and server: the client knows how to create valid data, and the server knows the rules that govern it.
sections.eli5: YANG is the form with boxes and rules, like a field that only accepts a number from 1 to 65535. Both sides agree to fill it in the same way.

sections.title: Extending Models and Translating YANG
sections.content:
One YANG module can augment another, adding elements from its own namespace into the first module's hierarchy. A vendor can therefore extend a standard OSPF module with vendor-specific leafs, and a client asking for an OSPF area receives the sub-hierarchy complete with the augmented data.

YANG also has companion forms. YIN is an XML grammar for YANG, so ordinary XML parsers can be used; conversion is direct, loss-less and reversible. YANG can also be mapped to Document Schema Definition Languages, of which RELAX NG is a major part (RFC 6110), to validate NETCONF content. Common data types are in RFC 6021, and IETF authoring guidelines are in RFC 6087.
sections.eli5: Anyone can staple an extra page onto the standard form without tearing it. YIN is the same form written in a different alphabet that more tools can read.

sections.title: How a Solution Works in Practice
sections.content:
In a typical solution the server holds YANG module definitions as meta-data for its NETCONF engine. The client opens a session, both sides exchange <hello> messages listing capabilities, and the client sends an operation inside an <rpc> element. The server parses it, checks it against the data model, performs it and replies in an <rpc-reply> element. The RFC adds that nobody is required to process modules generically: a server may hard code the model, and a client may be a simple shell script that fills an XML template.

The RFC lists how this answers the operator requirements: transactions, separating configuration from state data, deltas, dump and restore, network-wide commit and confirmed-commit, and full coverage of device abilities without scraping the command line.

It also describes roles. Modelers, reviewers, device developers and application developers each use the modules differently, and applications may be hard coded, bottom-up (generic, like a MIB browser) or top-down (their own model, transformed per device).
sections.eli5: The app says hello, asks for something using the agreed form, and the device checks the form, does the job and writes back.

sections.title: Modeling Considerations
sections.content:
On default values, the device MUST operationally behave as if a leaf were present with its default value. Devices may keep explicit defaults, trim them away, or report all of them, so clients must be ready for default leafs to be absent. The with-defaults capability (RFC 6243) lets the client choose.

On compliance, modelers should maximize the number of devices that can faithfully implement a model and can use feature and deviation to allow partial support. Both sides should still treat the module as a contract.

On data distinctions, the operators wanted configuration data, operational state and statistics kept separate, but NETCONF lumps the last two together as state data. The RFC states that the only viable solution at that time is to model configuration and operational values separately, for example distinct leafs duplex and op-duplex, one with config true and one with config false.
sections.eli5: What you asked for and what the device is really doing can differ, like a thermostat set to 20 degrees while the room is at 18. Keep both numbers in separate boxes.

items.desc: Retrieve all or part of a configuration datastore.

items.label: lock
items.desc: Prevent changes to a datastore from another party.

items.desc: Release a lock on a datastore.
